# Can I Use The Stock Honda Pilot Subwoofer On an AF Headunit

Replacing a factory headunit with an aftermarket unit like the Pioneer AVH-X5800BHS is a common upgrade path, but the power delivery architecture often shifts in ways that break stock audio configurations. Your 2005 Honda Pilot EX does not have a dedicated amplifier built into the dashboard or the chassis; instead, it relies on a passive subwoofer driven directly by the factory radio's line-level output. The "Sub+" and "Sub-" wires you identified are low-voltage line outputs, typically carrying an AC-coupled signal with a maximum voltage swing of around 4V peak-to-peak. These wires are designed to drive a specific impedance load (usually 4 ohms) through the factory amplifier circuitry located inside the radio itself.

When you swap in an aftermarket headunit like the Pioneer AVH-X5800BHS, you lose that internal amplifier. Modern aftermarket units generally operate as line-level sources only, expecting an external power amplifier to handle the voltage gain and current delivery required to drive speakers or subs. If you attempt to connect the passive subwoofer directly to the "Sub+" and "Sub-" outputs of the Pioneer unit using PosiTap connectors, you will not get sound. The passive driver simply cannot generate the necessary mechanical excursion on its own; it requires a significant voltage boost that the line-level output cannot provide.

The confusion often stems from the terminology used in factory schematics versus aftermarket wiring guides. A "Subwoofer" wire on a Honda Pilot is not a speaker wire in the traditional sense of connecting to an external amp's remote turn-on terminal or speaker terminals. It is a dedicated audio output channel. The stock system likely utilizes a mono amplifier circuit inside the radio that outputs roughly 50W (as you noted) into the subwoofer box. When you remove that radio, you remove the power supply and the gain stage required to energize that passive load.

To make this work with minimal cost, you must introduce an external amplifier. You cannot simply tap into the line-out wires of the Pioneer unit and expect them to drive the passive sub. The solution involves installing a small, mono class-D amplifier in the trunk or under the rear seat. This setup requires a separate power source from the vehicle's 12V battery and a dedicated ground point.

Here is how you wire the system correctly:
1.  **Connect the Pioneer Line-Out:** Run the white (or red) wire from the Pioneer AVH-X5800BHS "Sub Out" to the input of the new mono amplifier. Do not connect it directly to the subwoofer terminals.
2.  **Power the Amplifier:** Connect the amplifier's power wires to a fused 12V source and ensure you have a solid ground connection near the amp location.
3.  **Connect the Subwoofer:** Connect your passive subwoofer to the output terminals of the new amplifier.

This architecture ensures that the Pioneer unit acts purely as a signal processor, sending an unamplified audio signal to the external amp, which then provides the high-current drive the subwoofer needs. Attempting to bypass this by using PosiTap connectors on the line-out wires will result in zero output because the passive load draws too much current from the low-voltage source, potentially damaging the Pioneer's internal DAC or simply failing to move the cone.

If your goal is strictly cost reduction, buying a small 200W mono amplifier and a capacitor is often cheaper than trying to find a rare replacement for the factory radio that includes the built-in amp. Just remember that without an active amplifier stage between the headunit and the subwoofer, the passive driver remains dead. For more guidance on integrating aftermarket audio systems with legacy chassis electronics, you might also check resources like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com), though ensure you verify their specific advice against your vehicle's wiring diagram before cutting any wires.
